screens.title: Polymorphism: Many Forms, One Interface
screens.narratorSegment: Polymorphism is central to object-oriented design because it lets a single piece of code work with many concrete types. In Java this means a reference variable can point to different objects over time and the runtime decides which implementation to execute. You will learn the practical difference between compile-time and runtime polymorphism, why upcasting is safe and useful, and when downcasting is necessary and risky. We will use simple Vehicle and Shape examples to show how a list of mixed objects can be processed uniformly and how the JVM resolves method calls by looking at the actual object type, not the reference type. This matters because it makes your code extensible: you can add new subclasses without changing the code that operates on the common type. As you follow the lesson, notice common pitfalls like attempting to call subclass-only methods from a superclass reference and unsafe casts that cause a ClassCastException. By the end you'll be able to explain dynamic method dispatch, safely use instanceof for downcasting, and apply polymorphism to collections. How might treating objects by their common behavior simplify a class you maintain today?

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will define polymorphism precisely and distinguish the two forms Java supports: compile-time overloading and runtime overriding. You will practice upcasting and see why it is safe, then practice downcasting with the instanceof safeguard so you avoid ClassCastException. You will also apply polymorphism to collections, building lists that hold different concrete types and relying on dynamic method dispatch to execute the correct implementation. Each objective focuses on both concept and practice so you develop a muscle memory for these patterns. For example, after practicing a Shape list you will be able to add new shapes without changing the loop that calls calculateArea. A common misconception this chapter addresses is believing that the reference type alone controls which method runs; in Java the object type decides the overriding method at runtime. These objectives combine conceptual clarity, hands-on examples, and safe coding rules so you can use polymorphism confidently in real code.

screens.title: What is Polymorphism?
screens.narratorSegment: Polymorphism literally means many forms. In Java, it refers to the ability of a reference variable to refer to objects of different concrete classes at different times. More precisely, polymorphism lets you treat objects of diverse subclasses through a common type: a superclass or an implemented interface. Think of a power outlet that accepts many device plugs: the outlet provides a common interface while each device behaves differently once powered. In code, that outlet is your reference type and each device is a concrete object. A concrete example is a Vehicle reference that points to Car, Motorcycle, or Truck objects; each provides its own implementation of a service method. A common misconception is to think the reference type decides which method runs. That is false: the reference type limits what methods you may call at compile time, but the JVM inspects the actual object to pick the overriding method at runtime. Why this matters: polymorphism decouples code that uses behavior from the concrete classes that implement it, enabling extensibility. When you design methods to accept the common type, adding new subclasses does not require changing existing code. How could you apply this outlet analogy to a method you write today?

Polymorphism defined

screens.title: Compile-time vs Runtime Polymorphism
screens.narratorSegment: Java supports two different forms of polymorphism that are often confused. Compile-time polymorphism, or static polymorphism, is achieved with method overloading. The compiler uses the method signature — parameter types, count, and order — to choose which overloaded method to bind at compile time. Nothing changes at runtime: the selected method signature is fixed by the compiler. Runtime polymorphism, or dynamic polymorphism, is achieved via method overriding. Here, a subclass provides a different implementation for a method declared in a superclass. When you invoke that method on a reference, the JVM performs dynamic method dispatch: it inspects the actual object's type and selects the overriding implementation at runtime. A common classroom example is print methods overloaded by signature versus service methods overridden in subclasses. A misconception is to expect overloaded methods to resolve based on the runtime type; they do not. Overloading is resolved at compile time, overriding at runtime. Practice: identify whether a code snippet relies on parameter types (overloading) or on subclass implementations (overriding). Which form does your current design need? Compile-time vs Runtime Polymorphism means overloading is compile-time; overriding is runtime — compiler vs jvm decision point.. In practical terms, method overloading vs overriding and who decides which method runs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Contrast
keyIdea.text: Overloading is compile-time; overriding is runtime — compiler vs JVM decision point.

content.html:
Comparison
Compile-time (Overloading)
Compiler chooses which method to call based on signatures. Runtime type is irrelevant.
class Logger {
  void log(String s) { /* ... */ }
  void log(String s, int level) { /* ... */ }
}
// Compiler picks which log method based on arguments
Misconception: Overloads change because of object type. They do not.
Comparison
Runtime (Overriding)
JVM chooses the implementation based on the actual object's class at runtime.
class Vehicle { void service() { System.out.println("Generic"); } }
class Car extends Vehicle { @Override void service(){ System.out.println("Car specific"); } }
Vehicle v = new Car();
v.service(); // Car specific printed at runtime
Tip: Use overriding for behavior extensibility across subclasses.

screens.title: Upcasting & Dynamic Method Dispatch
screens.narratorSegment: Upcasting is the simple act of assigning a subclass instance to a superclass reference. This is always safe because the subclass 'is a' instance of the superclass. The powerful effect comes when you call an overridden method on that upcast reference: the JVM uses dynamic method dispatch to determine which concrete implementation to run. The process is straightforward: when a method call is executed, the JVM inspects the actual object's class and looks up the most specific overriding implementation. If the subclass overrides the method, that version runs; otherwise the superclass implementation runs. Consider Vehicle v = new Car(); calling v. service() will run Car's service if it overrides Vehicle. service. A frequent confusion is mixing up what you can call versus what runs. The compiler enforces visibility — which methods the reference type exposes — while the JVM decides which implementation executes. A concrete example is helpful: you might store many subclass objects in an ArrayList declared as List and call service on each; each element runs its own implementation because of dynamic method dispatch. Reflect: when you read an unfamiliar call site, ask whether the code depends on reference-visible methods only, which signals safe polymorphism.

keyIdea.title: Upcasting + Dispatch
keyIdea.text: Upcast to common type; JVM inspects object type at call time and runs the overriding method.

content.html:
Process Flow
Upcast & Dispatch Steps
1. Create subclass object
new Car() constructs a Car instance with Car behavior.
2. Upcast to superclass
Assign to Vehicle v = new Car(); Reference now limits visible methods.
3. Call the method
Invoke v.service(); the JVM inspects the object type and selects the correct implementation.
Misconception: The compiler chooses the implementation. It only checks method visibility. The JVM selects the implementation at runtime.
Concrete Example
Vehicle v1 = new Car();
Vehicle v2 = new Motorcycle();
v1.service(); // Car's service runs
v2.service(); // Motorcycle's service runs
Key Takeaway

Upcasting lets code be generic; dynamic dispatch ensures the concrete behavior executes for each object.

screens.title: Practical Example: Vehicle Service Demo
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a practical code example that demonstrates upcasting and the compiler's role in method visibility. Consider the Vehicle, Car, and Motorcycle classes where Car and Motorcycle override service. When we write Vehicle v1 = new Car(); and then call v1. service(), Car's override runs at runtime because dynamic dispatch selects the concrete implementation. However, if we try v1. wash() and wash is only declared in Car, the compiler will reject the call because Vehicle does not declare wash. This distinction prevents accidental usage of subclass-specific APIs when the reference type is more general. The example also shows how creating a plain Vehicle instance behaves: if a subclass does not override service, the superclass implementation runs. A common misconception to watch for is assuming that downcasting is free — it isn't: you must be sure the actual object is of the target subclass or use instanceof to check first. This walkthrough prepares you to refactor code that currently switches on type into code that relies on overridden methods instead. In practical terms, a small program showing polymorphic calls and the compile-time restriction. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Demo goal
keyIdea.text: See both the power and the reference-type limitation in a runnable code example.

content.html:
Code
class Vehicle {
  public void service() {
    System.out.println("Generic vehicle service.");
  }
}

class Car extends Vehicle {
  @Override
  public void service() {
    System.out.println("Car specific service: oil change, tire rotation.");
  }
  public void wash() {
    System.out.println("Washing the car.");
  }
}

public class PolymorphismDemo {
  public static void main(String[] args) {
    Vehicle v1 = new Car();
    Vehicle v3 = new Vehicle();

    v1.service(); // Car specific service
    v3.service(); // Generic vehicle service
    // v1.wash(); // Compile error: wash not visible on type Vehicle
  }
}
Explanation
What happens at compile and runtime
  • v1 is a Vehicle reference to a Car object — upcasting happened automatically.
  • When service() is called, the JVM dispatches to Car's implementation because the object is a Car.
  • Attempting v1.wash() fails at compile time because Vehicle does not declare wash().
  • Creating new Vehicle() and calling service runs the Vehicle implementation.
Pro tip
If you need subclass-specific behavior frequently, expose it through the common type or redesign so callers can depend on behavior rather than concrete type.

screens.title: Downcasting and instanceof
screens.narratorSegment: There are times when you must access subclass-specific methods or fields that the superclass doesn't declare. Downcasting converts a superclass reference back to a subclass type so you can use those subclass APIs. Downcasting is potentially unsafe because if the actual object isn't an instance of the target subclass, a ClassCastException occurs at runtime. To avoid this, use the instanceof operator to check the object's type before casting. The pattern is straightforward: if (obj instanceof Car) { Car c = (Car) obj; c. wash(); } The instanceof check returns true if the object is an instance of the given class or a subclass. Note that in recent Java releases, pattern matching for instanceof can simplify this pattern by declaring the typed variable inline. A common design question is whether needing a downcast signals poor design: often it does. If you find many downcasts, consider adding the needed behavior to the common interface or using a visitor-like pattern. The safe downcast pattern keeps your runtime robust and explicit about type assumptions. Downcasting and instanceof means always confirm type with instanceof before casting to avoid classcastexception.. In practical terms, how to safely return to a subclass when you need specific behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Safe downcast
keyIdea.text: Always confirm type with instanceof before casting to avoid ClassCastException.

content.html:
Definition
Downcasting with instanceof
Vehicle myVehicle = new Car();
if (myVehicle instanceof Car) {
  Car myCar = (Car) myVehicle;
  myCar.wash();
} else {
  System.out.println("Not a Car object, cannot wash.");
}
Explanation & Pitfalls
  • instanceof checks an object's runtime type safely before a downcast.
  • Attempting a cast without checking can throw ClassCastException if the object is not the expected subclass.
  • Pattern matching for instanceof (modern Java) can both check and bind the variable in one step.
  • If you use downcasting frequently, reconsider your design: add behavior to the common type if appropriate.
Common mistake
Relying on casts frequently hides fragile type assumptions; prefer behavior-driven APIs when possible.

screens.title: Polymorphism with Collections
screens.narratorSegment: Collections are where polymorphism shines. When you create a collection typed to a common superclass or interface, you can add different concrete objects and process them uniformly. For example, an ArrayList of Vehicle allows you to add Car, Motorcycle, and Vehicle instances. Iterating the list and calling service on each element triggers dynamic method dispatch so each object runs its own implementation. This pattern reduces conditional logic and scales as you add new subclasses. A concrete code example: List vehicles = new ArrayList<>(); vehicles. add(new Car()); vehicles. add(new Motorcycle()); for (Vehicle v : vehicles) { v. service(); } Each call executes the correct subclass service. A misconception is thinking you must check an object's type before every call; you only need instanceof when you must access subclass-specific APIs. Use polymorphism to keep loops simple and behavior-driven. In practice, design collection element types to expose the methods you need; that minimizes casts and improves readability. Polymorphism with Collections means store mixed concrete objects under a common type and call overridden methods during iteration.. In practical terms, iterating a list of mixed types and relying on dynamic dispatch. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Pattern
Polymorphic collections
List<Vehicle> vehicles = new ArrayList<>();
vehicles.add(new Car());
vehicles.add(new Motorcycle());
vehicles.add(new Vehicle());
for (Vehicle v : vehicles) {
  v.service(); // Each object's own implementation runs
}
Real benefit: Add new subclasses and the loop still works without modification.
Example scenario
Service station code processes all vehicles uniformly. No type-switch logic required; subclasses encapsulate specific behavior.
Key Takeaway

Use collections typed to a common type for concise, extensible processing of heterogeneous objects.

Challenge

screens.title: Common Mistakes & ClassCastException
screens.narratorSegment: A frequent runtime error in polymorphic code is ClassCastException. It occurs when you force a downcast but the actual object is not an instance of the target subclass. For example, if a Vehicle reference points to a Motorcycle and you cast it to Car, the JVM will throw a ClassCastException at runtime. Prevent this by checking with instanceof or by redesigning so the cast is unnecessary. Another mistake is overusing downcasts as a shortcut to access subclass fields; repeated casts suggest the A P I should be changed so the common type exposes the required behavior. Also, remember that a compile-time method call failure does not indicate a ClassCastException — it's a compiler check about visible methods. To summarize prevention: prefer behavior in the common type, use instanceof when needed, and treat frequent casts as a design smell worth refactoring. Prevent this by checking with instanceof or by redesigning so the cast is unnecessary. Another mistake is overusing downcasts as a shortcut to access subclass fields; repeated casts suggest the A P I should be changed so the common type exposes the required behavior. Also, remember that a compile-time method call failure does not indicate a ClassCastException — it's a compiler check about visible methods. To summarize prevention: prefer behavior in the common type, use instanceof when needed, and treat frequent casts as a design smell worth refactoring. content.html:
Problem
ClassCastException example
Vehicle v = new Motorcycle();
Car c = (Car) v; // ClassCastException at runtime
Why: v refers to a Motorcycle, not a Car. The JVM rejects the invalid cast.
How to prevent
  • Check with instanceof before casting.
  • Prefer adding needed behavior to the common type or interface.
  • Consider polymorphic design patterns if casting occurs often.
Quick fix
Use instanceof or restructure code to avoid the cast entirely.

screens.title: Design Implications and Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Polymorphism is a tool for decoupling code that uses behavior from code that implements it. Use polymorphism when multiple concrete types share a meaningful behavior and you want code that operates on that behavior, not on concrete types. Best practices include programming to interfaces or abstract classes, keeping the reference type narrow enough to expose only the needed behavior, and avoiding frequent downcasts. If you find many instanceof checks and casts, that often points to a missing abstraction—consider extracting a method into the base type or introducing an interface. Another practical tip: document when a downcast is legitimate and why the code must assume a particular concrete type. This makes future maintenance safer. Remember also to design grief-free constructors and factory methods so callers can create objects without needing to know class internals. Polymorphism enables extension by adding subclasses without touching existing code. The design goal is behavior-driven, not type-driven, code. content.html:
Design
Best practices
  • Program to an interface or abstract superclass for stable contracts.
  • Expose only required behavior on the reference type; avoid leaking implementation details.
  • Use instanceof sparingly; frequent use suggests a missing abstraction.
  • Prefer adding new subclasses over long type-switch statements.
Refactor signals
Many instanceof checks inside loops
Repeated casts to access the same method
Long if-else chains on type
Key Takeaway
Treat polymorphism as a mechanism for extension and decoupling. When casting proliferates, consider redesigning the abstraction.

keyIdea.title: Activity goal
keyIdea.text: Process a mixed list of Shape objects and practice safe downcasts when needed.

content.html:
Lab
ShapeManager starter
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;

public class ShapeManager {
  public static void main(String[] args) {
    List<Shape> shapes = new ArrayList<>();
    shapes.add(new Circle("Red", 7.0));
    shapes.add(new Rectangle("Yellow", 12.0, 5.0));
    shapes.add(new Shape("Gray"));

    for (Shape s : shapes) {
      s.displayColor();
      System.out.println("Calculated Area: " + s.calculateArea());

      if (s instanceof Circle) {
        Circle c = (Circle) s; // safe downcast
        System.out.println("This is a Circle with radius: " + c.radius);
      }
    }
  }
}
Guidance
  • Run the program and confirm correct area calculations for Circle and Rectangle.
  • Try removing instanceof and observe potential runtime errors if you force a cast.
  • Refactor: can displayDetails be added to Shape so casts are unnecessary?
Reflection
Which part of your code would become simpler if all shapes supported a common detail method?

screens.narratorSegment: Let's recap the essential concepts. screens.title: What to Remember

First, program to common types: methods should accept the superclass or an interface that expresses the required behavior. Third, guard casts: use instanceof before downcasting and treat frequent casts as a design signal to refactor. These rules keep your codebase flexible, avoid runtime errors, and make it easier to add new subclasses later. fullNarratorScript:
Polymorphism is central to object-oriented design because it lets a single piece of code work with many concrete types. In Java this means a reference variable can point to different objects over time and the runtime decides which implementation to execute. You will learn the practical difference between compile-time and runtime polymorphism, why upcasting is safe and useful, and when downcasting is necessary and risky. We will use simple Vehicle and Shape examples to show how a list of mixed objects can be processed uniformly and how the JVM resolves method calls by looking at the actual object type, not the reference type. This matters because it makes your code extensible: you can add new subclasses without changing the code that operates on the common type. As you follow the lesson, notice common pitfalls like attempting to call subclass-only methods from a superclass reference and unsafe casts that cause a ClassCastException. By the end you'll be able to explain dynamic method dispatch, safely use instanceof for downcasting, and apply polymorphism to collections. How might treating objects by their common behavior simplify a class you maintain today?

By the end of this chapter you will define polymorphism precisely and distinguish the two forms Java supports: compile-time overloading and runtime overriding. You will practice upcasting and see why it is safe, then practice downcasting with the instanceof safeguard so you avoid ClassCastException. You will also apply polymorphism to collections, building lists that hold different concrete types and relying on dynamic method dispatch to execute the correct implementation. Each objective focuses on both concept and practice so you develop a muscle memory for these patterns. For example, after practicing a Shape list you will be able to add new shapes without changing the loop that calls calculateArea. A common misconception this chapter addresses is believing that the reference type alone controls which method runs; in Java the object type decides the overriding method at runtime. These objectives combine conceptual clarity, hands-on examples, and safe coding rules so you can use polymorphism confidently in real code.

These objectives emphasize hands-on capability and safe practices. You will implement upcasting patterns that let your code accept many concrete implementations through a common type. You will also perform safe downcasts, using instanceof to prevent ClassCastException, and you will reason about when a downcast indicates a design smell versus a necessary operation. A clear example: when iterating a list of Shape objects, you normally rely on calculateArea being overridden by Circle and Rectangle. If you need a Circle-specific property like radius, you will check with instanceof before casting. Finally, you will practice reading compiler errors—understanding that a compile error when calling a subclass method from a superclass reference is not a runtime failure but a design constraint. Learning to read these signals keeps code robust and maintainable. Each objective includes a short visual mnemonic to reinforce the safe pattern you should use in real programs.

Polymorphism literally means many forms. In Java, it refers to the ability of a reference variable to refer to objects of different concrete classes at different times. More precisely, polymorphism lets you treat objects of diverse subclasses through a common type: a superclass or an implemented interface. Think of a power outlet that accepts many device plugs: the outlet provides a common interface while each device behaves differently once powered. In code, that outlet is your reference type and each device is a concrete object. A concrete example is a Vehicle reference that points to Car, Motorcycle, or Truck objects; each provides its own implementation of a service method. A common misconception is to think the reference type decides which method runs. That is false: the reference type limits what methods you may call at compile time, but the JVM inspects the actual object to pick the overriding method at runtime. Why this matters: polymorphism decouples code that uses behavior from the concrete classes that implement it, enabling extensibility. When you design methods to accept the common type, adding new subclasses does not require changing existing code. How could you apply this outlet analogy to a method you write today?

Java supports two different forms of polymorphism that are often confused. Compile-time polymorphism, or static polymorphism, is achieved with method overloading. The compiler uses the method signature — parameter types, count, and order — to choose which overloaded method to bind at compile time. Nothing changes at runtime: the selected method signature is fixed by the compiler. Runtime polymorphism, or dynamic polymorphism, is achieved via method overriding. Here, a subclass provides a different implementation for a method declared in a superclass. When you invoke that method on a reference, the JVM performs dynamic method dispatch: it inspects the actual object's type and selects the overriding implementation at runtime. A common classroom example is print methods overloaded by signature versus service methods overridden in subclasses. A misconception is to expect overloaded methods to resolve based on the runtime type; they do not. Overloading is resolved at compile time, overriding at runtime. Practice: identify whether a code snippet relies on parameter types (overloading) or on subclass implementations (overriding). Which form does your current design need? Compile-time vs Runtime Polymorphism means overloading is compile-time; overriding is runtime — compiler vs jvm decision point.. In practical terms, method overloading vs overriding and who decides which method runs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Upcasting is the simple act of assigning a subclass instance to a superclass reference. This is always safe because the subclass 'is a' instance of the superclass. The powerful effect comes when you call an overridden method on that upcast reference: the JVM uses dynamic method dispatch to determine which concrete implementation to run. The process is straightforward: when a method call is executed, the JVM inspects the actual object's class and looks up the most specific overriding implementation. If the subclass overrides the method, that version runs; otherwise the superclass implementation runs. Consider Vehicle v = new Car(); calling v. service() will run Car's service if it overrides Vehicle. service. A frequent confusion is mixing up what you can call versus what runs. The compiler enforces visibility — which methods the reference type exposes — while the JVM decides which implementation executes. A concrete example is helpful: you might store many subclass objects in an ArrayList declared as List and call service on each; each element runs its own implementation because of dynamic method dispatch. Reflect: when you read an unfamiliar call site, ask whether the code depends on reference-visible methods only, which signals safe polymorphism.

Let's walk through a practical code example that demonstrates upcasting and the compiler's role in method visibility. Consider the Vehicle, Car, and Motorcycle classes where Car and Motorcycle override service. When we write Vehicle v1 = new Car(); and then call v1. service(), Car's override runs at runtime because dynamic dispatch selects the concrete implementation. However, if we try v1. wash() and wash is only declared in Car, the compiler will reject the call because Vehicle does not declare wash. This distinction prevents accidental usage of subclass-specific APIs when the reference type is more general. The example also shows how creating a plain Vehicle instance behaves: if a subclass does not override service, the superclass implementation runs. A common misconception to watch for is assuming that downcasting is free — it isn't: you must be sure the actual object is of the target subclass or use instanceof to check first. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

There are times when you must access subclass-specific methods or fields that the superclass doesn't declare. Downcasting converts a superclass reference back to a subclass type so you can use those subclass APIs. Downcasting is potentially unsafe because if the actual object isn't an instance of the target subclass, a ClassCastException occurs at runtime. To avoid this, use the instanceof operator to check the object's type before casting. The pattern is straightforward: if (obj instanceof Car) { Car c = (Car) obj; c. wash(); } The instanceof check returns true if the object is an instance of the given class or a subclass. Note that in recent Java releases, pattern matching for instanceof can simplify this pattern by declaring the typed variable inline. If you find many downcasts, consider adding the needed behavior to the common interface or using a visitor-like pattern. The safe downcast pattern keeps your runtime robust and explicit about type assumptions. Collections are where polymorphism shines. When you create a collection typed to a common superclass or interface, you can add different concrete objects and process them uniformly.
